Introduction

The modern liberal order rests on a simple proposition, articulated most famously by John Stuart Mill: "Over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign." The state may restrict liberty only to prevent harm to others—not to enforce majority morality, not to protect adults from their own choices, and not to codify religious or cultural disgust.

This principle has successfully dismantled laws against interracial marriage, sodomy, adultery, fornication, and same-sex relationships. In Lawrence v. Texas (2003), the U.S. Supreme Court held that the state cannot criminalize private, consensual adult sexual conduct simply because the majority finds it immoral. Justice Kennedy wrote that liberty "presumes an autonomy of self that includes freedom of thought, belief, expression, and certain intimate conduct."

If this principle is valid—and virtually every defender of reproductive rights, LGBTQ+ rights, and sexual privacy insists it is—then it cannot be abandoned the moment its logic leads somewhere uncomfortable. A principle applied only when convenient is no principle at all.

Consent Is the Only Morally Relevant Standard

In a free society, the determining question about any sexual relationship between adults is whether all parties have given informed, uncoerced consent. Consent is what distinguishes sex from assault, marriage from servitude, intimacy from exploitation. It is the lodestar of modern sexual ethics.

Consenting adult siblings, cousins, or other relatives who form romantic or sexual bonds have violated no one's autonomy. They have not assaulted anyone, defrauded anyone, or breached any legitimate contract. To jail them is to jail people for the configuration of their private affections—a category of offense that, on reflection, ought not to exist in a liberal polity.

Critics often respond that family relationships involve inherent power imbalances that vitiate consent. But this argument proves too much. Power asymmetries exist in virtually all relationships—between employers and employees, teachers and former students, wealthy and poor partners, older and younger lovers. We do not criminalize these relationships wholesale; we address genuine coercion where it exists. The law already prohibits abuse, grooming, and sexual activity with minors. These prohibitions do the necessary moral work. A sweeping ban on consensual adult relationships sweeps up innocent people to avoid the harder task of distinguishing coercion from choice.

The Harm Principle Fails to Justify Criminalization

Defenders of incest laws typically invoke three harms: genetic risk to offspring, family dysfunction, and moral corruption of society. Each collapses under scrutiny.

Genetic risk. Studies suggest modestly elevated risks of recessive genetic conditions in children of first-degree relatives, but the risk for first cousins is comparable to that of women conceiving after age 40. We do not criminalize reproduction by carriers of Huntington's disease, Tay-Sachs, or cystic fibrosis. We do not prohibit older women from having children. To single out related couples for criminal prosecution on eugenic grounds is both inconsistent and ethically troubling, given eugenics' monstrous history. Moreover, this objection has no application whatsoever to same-sex relatives, post-reproductive adults, or couples using contraception—yet the laws criminalize them all.

Family dysfunction. The claim that such relationships damage families is largely circular: they damage families in part because society stigmatizes and criminalizes them. Families are also disrupted by affairs, estrangements, religious conversions, and political disagreements—none of which we criminalize. Private pain is not a basis for public prosecution.

Moral corruption. This is simply the enforcement of majoritarian disgust, which Lawrence and the broader liberal tradition explicitly reject as a legitimate basis for criminal law. Disgust is not an argument. It is the feeling that once justified laws against interracial marriage and homosexuality, and we rightly regard those laws as unjust today.

Incest laws are not dead letters. In Germany, Patrick Stübing was imprisoned for years for his consensual relationship with his adult sister, from whom he had been separated in childhood and met only as an adult. The European Court of Human Rights upheld his conviction, but the case drew a powerful dissent and a report from the German Ethics Council in 2014 recommending decriminalization. Similar prosecutions occur in the United States, where adult siblings and other relatives have faced felony charges, sex-offender registration, and imprisonment.

These punishments destroy lives, break up families that wished to remain intact, and criminalize people whose only offense is loving someone the majority disapproves of. The cost is not hypothetical—it is borne by real people right now.

Conclusion: The Courage of Consistency

Defending unpopular applications of a principle is the price of holding the principle at all. A society that tells gay couples, interracial couples, unmarried couples, and kink practitioners that their private lives are their own business cannot coherently reserve the power to imprison other consenting adults for their private intimate choices. It is not the proper role of the criminal law. Liberty worth having is liberty extended to those whose choices we would not make for ourselves. Decriminalizing consensual adult incest is not an endorsement of incest; it is an acknowledgment that the state's coercive power has no legitimate place in the bedrooms of adults who have harmed no one.

To criminalize a private, consensual act between adults is to treat them as property of the state or of a collective moral code, stripping them of agency over their own desires and personhood. If a woman has the right to terminate a pregnancy, if a person has the right to engage in BDSM, if individuals have the right to marry a stranger from across the globe, then the logic of bodily autonomy demands they also have the right to share intimacy with a sibling or parent, assuming all parties are competent, consenting adults. Closely linked is the principle of consent. Consent is the sole moral and legal criterion that can transform an act from assault to intimacy. In a consensual incestuous relationship between adults, all participants have given their full, knowing, and voluntary agreement. The law’s recognition of consent as the boundary for permissible sexual activity is what separates healthy sexuality from violence. This is the same flawed logic used to deny LGBTQ+ individuals the right to marry, claiming their consent was somehow "compromised" by their nature. First, the genetic argument. It is true that children of closely related parents face significantly higher risks of severe genetic disorders. However, this is an argument for education, genetic counseling, and access to contraception or abortion—not for criminal law. We do not outlaw reproduction for people with heritable diseases, nor do we ban people over 40 from having children due to increased risks. We address the consequences (a potential child’s welfare) through social services and medical support, not by criminalizing the precondition of the relationship. To criminalize the relationship itself is a disproportionate and ineffective response. It punishes the adults for a risk, not an actual harm. To maintain these laws is to prioritize social comfort over individual liberty, to substitute the state’s moral judgment for personal sovereignty, and to perpetuate a system where the government can punish you not for what you do, but for who you are related to. The path of true liberty is often uncomfortable, but it is the only path a just society can walk. Decriminalization is not the end of morality; it is the beginning of a morality that respects the freedom of all individuals to define the meaning of their own lives.

The Liberty Principle Applied: A Case for Decriminalizing Consensual Adult Incest

An Academic Persuasive Essay

Introduction

Few legal questions test our commitment to individual liberty as starkly as this one. The criminal prohibition of consensual sexual relationships between closely related adults exists in most Western legal systems, yet it sits uneasily alongside the foundational principles those systems claim to uphold: personal autonomy, bodily sovereignty, equal treatment under law, and the strict limitation of state power to situations involving demonstrable harm. This is not an argument that such relationships are wise, healthy, or admirable. It is an argument that the state lacks justification for deploying its most coercive instrument—criminal punishment—against adults whose private, consensual conduct harms no identifiable third party.

I. The Harm Principle: The Foundation of Criminal Law in a Free Society

John Stuart Mill's harm principle remains the bedrock of liberal jurisprudence: "The only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilized community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others." Every legitimate criminal prohibition in a liberal society must answer one essential question: who is being harmed against their will?

When both participants are competent adults who have given informed, voluntary consent, the answer is: no one. The state does not criminalize other forms of sexual conduct that many citizens find morally distasteful—adultery, promiscuity, various fetish practices—provided they occur between consenting adults. The burden falls on the state to demonstrate a compelling interest beyond communal disapproval. As we shall see, the traditional justifications offered for incest prohibitions each fail this test when applied narrowly to the class of cases under discussion: consensual, adult relationships.

II. The Autonomy Argument: Sovereignty Over One's Own Body and Relationships

The principle of bodily autonomy holds that competent adults possess the right to make decisions about their own bodies, including decisions about sexual intimacy, without state interference. This principle has been progressively vindicated across legal history:

  • Griswold v. Connecticut (1965) recognized the right of married couples to use contraception.
  • Eisenstadt v. Baird (1972) extended that right to unmarried individuals.
  • Lawrence v. Texas (2003) struck down sodomy laws, with Justice Kennedy writing that adults have the right "to engage in their conduct without intervention of the government" and that "the fact that the governing majority in a State has traditionally viewed a particular practice as immoral is not a sufficient reason for upholding a law."
  • Obergefell v. Hodges (2015) affirmed that intimate choices central to personal dignity and autonomy are protected.

Each of these rulings repudiated the notion that majoritarian moral disapproval alone can justify criminal sanctions on private, consensual adult conduct. The logic of these decisions does not conveniently stop at the boundaries of consanguinity. If two adults possess the cognitive capacity to consent, and do so freely, the nature of their genetic relationship does not alter the fundamental autonomy interest at stake.

To argue otherwise is to claim that the state owns a veto over the intimate lives of competent adults based not on what they do but on who they are in relation to each other—a principle more characteristic of caste systems than of liberal democracies.

III. Deconstructing the Traditional Justifications

Proponents of criminalization typically advance three arguments: genetic harm to offspring, the protection of family structure, and the prevention of exploitation. Each dissolves under careful analysis when constrained to the specific class of cases at issue.

A. The Genetic Argument

The most frequently cited justification is the increased risk of genetic disorders in offspring of closely related parents. This argument fails on multiple grounds:

  1. It is empirically overstated. While consanguineous reproduction does elevate the probability of autosomal recessive conditions, the absolute risk for a single-generation pairing between first-degree relatives is roughly comparable to the risk faced by women over 40 or by carriers of known genetic conditions—groups the state does not criminalize for reproducing. A study published in the Journal of Genetic Counseling found that the added risk of birth defects for first-cousin couples is approximately 1.7–2.8% above the baseline population risk of 3–4%. For closer relations the risk is higher, but remains a probability, not a certainty.

  2. It proves too much. If the state may criminalize sexual relationships that carry elevated genetic risk, then logically it may also criminalize reproduction by carriers of Huntington's disease, Tay-Sachs, cystic fibrosis, or other heritable conditions. No serious legal scholar or ethicist advocates such a policy, because we recognize it as eugenics—a project rightly discredited by history. We cannot consistently invoke genetic risk as a basis for criminal law in one context while repudiating it in all others.

  3. It conflates sex with reproduction. The criminalization is of the sexual act, not of reproduction. Many such relationships involve same-sex couples, post-menopausal individuals, or partners who use contraception or have been sterilized. Criminalizing sex itself because it might lead to reproduction with elevated genetic risk is wildly disproportionate. If the concern is genuinely about offspring, the appropriate response—if any is warranted—lies in genetic counseling or reproductive regulation, not in imprisoning people for the act of sex.

  4. Reproductive liberty is a recognized right. Courts have consistently held that the decision whether to bear children is constitutionally protected. The state does not conduct genetic screening as a precondition for sexual activity or reproduction for any other population.

B. The Family Structure Argument

Some argue that incestuous relationships destabilize family dynamics, confuse relational roles, and undermine the family as a social institution. This argument suffers from several weaknesses:

  1. It is speculative rather than empirical. There is scant rigorous evidence that the existence of a sexual relationship between, say, adult siblings who live independently fundamentally undermines the broader family unit in a way that should concern the criminal law. Families are disrupted by alcoholism, infidelity, estrangement, and countless other dynamics the state does not criminalize.

  2. It assumes a particular model of family. The argument presupposes that familial roles are fixed and that their disruption constitutes a harm severe enough to warrant imprisonment. Liberal societies have progressively abandoned the notion that the state may enforce a single template of family structure—this was a central insight of the movement for marriage equality.

  3. It applies general concerns to justify individual punishment. Even if some abstract harm to "family structure" could be demonstrated, criminal punishment falls on individuals. Justice requires that individuals be punished for concrete harms they cause, not for abstract threats to social institutions.

  4. The argument applies poorly to many real cases. Consider genetic siblings separated at birth who meet as adults (so-called genetic sexual attraction, or GSA). They share DNA but have no shared family structure to disrupt. Their situation exposes the hollowness of the family-structure rationale: the law punishes them identically to those raised together, revealing that the real operative force behind the prohibition is something other than concern for family dynamics.

C. The Exploitation and Power Dynamics Argument

This is the strongest objection, and it deserves respectful, careful treatment. The concern is that family relationships involve inherent power imbalances—particularly parent-child relationships—that make genuine consent impossible or suspect.

This concern is legitimate, but it does not justify a blanket criminal prohibition for several reasons:

  1. The law already addresses coercion and exploitation independently. Every jurisdiction possesses laws against sexual assault, rape, coercion, undue influence, and exploitation of vulnerable persons. These laws are precisely tailored to the actual harm (the vitiation of consent) and can be applied vigorously in any incestuous context where consent is compromised.

  2. A blanket ban is both overinclusive and underinclusive. It is overinclusive because it criminalizes relationships where no power imbalance exists (adult siblings of similar age, relatives who met as adults). It is underinclusive because it does nothing to address power-imbalanced relationships that are not consanguineous (employer-employee, professor-student, therapist-client, clergy-congregant, older partner-younger partner). If the concern is genuinely about power and consent, the remedy should target power and consent, not genetic relatedness.

  3. We do not criminalize other relationships with inherent power dynamics. An adult child may enter into a business partnership, a caretaking arrangement, or a financial agreement with a parent. These relationships involve the same power dynamics, yet the law does not declare all such agreements void and criminal. Instead, it applies doctrines of undue influence and duress where there is evidence that consent was compromised.

  4. Presuming the absence of consent infantilizes adults. To declare that an adult cannot consent to a particular relationship because of who the other person is—regardless of the actual circumstances—is to strip that adult of the agency the legal system otherwise assigns to them. A 35-year-old is legally competent to consent to surgery, to sign contracts, to join the military, and to engage in sexual relationships with any other willing adult. Declaring that same person legally incapable of consenting to a specific relationship, absent any evidence of coercion, is paternalism of the most extreme kind.

  5. The argument can be addressed through procedural safeguards rather than criminalization. If lawmakers are concerned about the potential for exploitation, less restrictive alternatives exist: mandatory waiting periods, counseling requirements, or evidentiary presumptions that shift the burden in cases where a pre-existing custodial relationship existed. These measures would address the legitimate concern while respecting the autonomy of genuinely consenting adults.

IV. The Disgust Problem: Moral Intuition Is Not a Basis for Criminal Law

Psychologist Jonathan Haidt's famous "dumbfounding" experiments placed this exact scenario before research subjects: two adult siblings, fully consenting, using contraception, experiencing no psychological harm. Subjects overwhelmingly condemned the behavior—but could not articulate a rational justification. They were, in Haidt's term, "morally dumbfounded." They knew it was wrong but could not explain why without invoking harms that had been stipulated away.

This research illuminates a crucial point: much of the opposition to decriminalization is driven not by reason but by the emotion of disgust. Disgust is a powerful moral intuition, but liberal democracies have learned—painfully, repeatedly—that disgust is an unreliable guide to justice:

  • Disgust sustained anti-miscegenation laws.
  • Disgust sustained the criminalization of homosexuality.
  • Disgust sustained bans on interreligious marriage.

In each case, the moral certainty of the majority eventually yielded to the recognition that visceral revulsion is not a harm, and that the rights of minorities cannot be put to a popular vote of aesthetic sensibility. As the philosopher Martha Nussbaum has argued extensively, disgust "has been used throughout history to exclude and subordinate groups," and it should be treated with the deepest suspicion as a basis for law.

If we cannot articulate a concrete, demonstrable harm—beyond "it disgusts me" or "it feels wrong"—then we do not have a justification for criminal punishment. We have only a prejudice.

V. Comparative and International Perspectives

It is instructive to note that several developed nations have already reached the conclusion this essay advocates:

  • France has had no criminal prohibition on consensual adult incest since the Napoleonic Code of 1810, operating for over two centuries without the social collapse predicted by prohibitionists.
  • Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Belgium, and Turkey similarly do not criminalize consensual adult incest.
  • Sweden permits sexual relationships between adult half-siblings.

VI. The Principled Consistency Argument

Perhaps the most compelling argument is one of simple consistency. Liberal democracies claim to operate on certain principles:

  1. Adults are sovereign over their own bodies.
  2. The state may not criminalize conduct solely because the majority finds it immoral.
  3. Criminal law requires a demonstrable harm to an identifiable victim.
  4. Laws must be rationally related to the harm they purport to prevent.
  5. The least restrictive means must be employed.

If we are sincere about these principles, we must apply them even—especially—when the result is uncomfortable. The measure of a society's commitment to liberty is not whether it protects popular freedoms but whether it protects unpopular ones. As Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote, "If there is any principle of the Constitution that more imperatively calls for attachment than any other, it is the principle of free thought—not free thought for those who agree with us but freedom for the thought we hate."

The same logic applies to freedom of action. A right to sexual autonomy that evaporates the moment it becomes uncomfortable is not a right at all—it is a privilege extended at the discretion of the majority. And privileges extended at the majority's discretion are precisely what constitutional rights exist to guard against.

VII. Addressing the "Slippery Slope" Objection

Critics will argue that decriminalization constitutes a step down a slippery slope. This objection is unpersuasive for two reasons:

  1. The consent boundary is firm and clear. The argument presented here rests entirely on the consent of competent adults. It does not extend to minors, to individuals with cognitive impairments that vitiate consent, or to any situation involving coercion. The criminal prohibition of consensual sexual relationships between closely related adults fails every test that a liberal society applies to its criminal laws.
